slides.title: The request before 5 PM
slides.objective: Establish the fictional cast and baseline decision
screen_text: A familiar name. A payment deadline.
What would you check?
slides.evidence: Farid receives Invoice MS-1048 at 16:42.
slides.interaction: Open the first message to show the full email.
slides.facilitator_notes: Say Meranti is fictional. Farid is the central character of the opening; Aina, Mei and Ravi are introduced as they appear. Open the email when the room has read the headline. Do not disclose the outcome.

slides.title: Today’s workshop
slides.objective: What we will practise today, in what order, and how we will work together.
screen_text: Spot when a message asks for money, information or access
Check requests through a route you already trust
Know what an approval, code or app permission really gives away
Report quickly and usefully, including your own mistakes
slides.facilitator_notes: Read the slide aloud briefly; it frames the module. No hidden content.
outcomes: Spot when a message asks for money, information or access
Check requests through a route you already trust
Know what an approval, code or app permission really gives away
Report quickly and usefully, including your own mistakes
rules: Everything in today’s story is fictional; real cases are labelled
Nobody needs to share a personal incident
Reporting is never blamed: thank people for speaking up
slides.what_this_shows: What we will practise today, in what order, and how we will work together.
slides.key_point: Today is about one habit: when a message asks for money, information or access, check it through a route you already trust.

slides.title: A request that fits the job
screen_text: What can this email actually prove?
slides.evidence: Nadia asks Farid to use changed bank details. Expected .example sender and destination.
slides.interaction: Expand sender and destination.
slides.reveal: A matching address does not prove who controls the account.
slides.facilitator_notes: Ask what changed and what must be verified. Use the prototype text.
slides.what_this_shows: Farid gets an expected invoice email from a known supplier, but the bank details have changed.
slides.key_point: A correct sender address and a familiar conversation do not prove who is writing. A change to bank details always needs an independent check.

slides.title: Another familiar name appears
slides.objective: Recognise pressure from an apparent manager
screen_text: Does this conversation give Farid enough confidence to pay?
slides.evidence: Ravi display name urges payment, then says he is in a meeting.
slides.interaction: Reveal messages one by one; replay.
slides.facilitator_notes: Ask what changed in the evidence. A display name is insufficient.
slides.what_this_shows: A chat using the manager’s name pushes Farid to pay quickly.
slides.key_point: A display name and urgency tell you nothing about who controls the account. Pressure to skip a check is a reason to slow down.

slides.title: What the two messages can prove
slides.objective: State what the email and the chat can and cannot prove
screen_text: A correct sender address and a familiar conversation do not prove who is writing.
A display name and urgency tell you nothing about who controls the account.
slides.interaction: Give the explanation after the room has answered both questions; then move to the decision.
slides.facilitator_notes: Explanation stage for scenes 01 and 02. Use the answers the room gave. Both points lead to the decision on the next slide.
slides.what_this_shows: Neither message proves who is asking. The bank change still needs an independent check.
slides.key_point: A correct sender address, a familiar conversation, a display name and urgency do not prove who is writing. A change to bank details always needs an independent check, and pressure to skip it is a reason to slow down.

slides.title: What should Farid do next?
screen_text: Choose an action.
What makes the verification route trustworthy?
slides.evidence: Expected invoice, changed bank details, manager pressure.
slides.interaction: Vote before selecting.
slides.reveal: Call the supplier’s established contact and follow normal approval.
slides.facilitator_notes: A genuine request would still need the same process.

options.label: Pay using revised details
options.feedback: The bank change remains unverified.

options.label: Reply to Nadia for confirmation
options.feedback: The same mailbox cannot provide an independent check.

options.label: Call the supplier using existing records
options.feedback: This gives an independent verification route.

slides.what_this_shows: Your first decision of the day. Vote with a show of hands, then select the answer the room chose.
slides.key_point: Verify through a contact you already hold, such as the supplier record, then follow the normal approval process. Replying to the same email cannot verify anything.

slides.title: The callback changes the picture
slides.objective: Separate original clues from newly verified facts
screen_text: The supplier denies the change.
Ravi denies sending the chat.
Farid holds the payment and reports.
slides.evidence: Same email as SL02.
slides.interaction: Reveal findings.
slides.reveal: Independent verification supplies new evidence.
slides.facilitator_notes: Do not imply participants should have guessed facts revealed only now. IT investigates account misuse.
slides.what_this_shows: Farid calls the supplier on the number already held in the finance system.
slides.key_point: Independent verification gives you facts the message never could. Hold the payment, keep the evidence and report.

slides.title: When the meeting looked convincing
slides.objective: Apply verification to a documented video fraud
screen_text: Approximate reported loss: HK$200m
Email, prerecorded video and payment messages
slides.evidence: Official January 2024 Hong Kong incident.
slides.interaction: Ask which independent check could interrupt the sequence.
slides.reveal: Use an independent authorised transaction workflow.
slides.facilitator_notes: Preserve prerecorded/no-interaction detail. No victim screenshot or invented dialogue.
slides.what_this_shows: A real case: a fabricated video meeting helped convince an employee to transfer about HK$200 million.
slides.key_point: Even a convincing meeting can be fabricated. A separate, authorised payment check is what stops the loss.

slides.title: Module 1: The borrowed identity
slides.objective: What this module covers and why it matters.
screen_text: Tell a copied profile from a genuine account someone else controls
Spot when a friendly conversation turns into a sensitive request
Respond if someone uses your name
slides.facilitator_notes: Read the slide aloud briefly; it frames the module. No hidden content.
slides.why: Anyone can copy a name, photo and job title, and messages that borrow a familiar identity get trusted.
outcomes: Tell a copied profile from a genuine account someone else controls
Spot when a friendly conversation turns into a sensitive request
Respond if someone uses your name
slides.what_this_shows: What this module covers and why it matters.
slides.key_point: Identity on a screen is easy to borrow. Verify the person through a route you already trust.

slides.title: Impersonation and phishing
screen_text: Impersonation
Phishing
Spear phishing
slides.evidence: One copied profile leads to a document invitation.
slides.interaction: Define the three words; the overlap follows on the next slide.
slides.reveal: The techniques can overlap.
slides.facilitator_notes: Keep terms plain. Definitions are course paraphrases.
slides.what_this_shows: Three words we use all day.
slides.key_point: Impersonation borrows a trusted identity; phishing asks you to act; spear phishing aims at you specifically.

slides.reveal: The techniques can overlap.
slides.interaction: Ask which concept describes each step.
slides.title: One message can do all three
slides.objective: Show how impersonation, spear phishing and phishing overlap in one attack
screen_text: One story, three steps
Which word describes each step?
slides.evidence: A fictional three-step story: a copied profile, targeted messages, a sign-in request.
slides.facilitator_notes: Keep terms plain. Ask the room to name the concept for each step before you do.
slides.what_this_shows: One fictional story in three steps. Which word describes each step?
slides.key_point: One message can do all three: borrow an identity, aim at you specifically and ask you to act.

slides.title: What can someone learn about Aina?
slides.objective: Identify public context used in persuasive messages
screen_text: Job title
Project announcement
Supplier and colleague names
slides.evidence: Fictional public profile and event post.
slides.interaction: Reveal public details; identify one that makes a message credible.
slides.reveal: Knowing workplace details does not prove employment or authority.
slides.facilitator_notes: Use only invented posts. Explain that public context can reduce suspicion without victim blame.
slides.what_this_shows: Everything on Aina’s public profile that a stranger could reuse.
slides.key_point: Public work details make a fake message feel expected. Knowing them does not prove the sender works with you.

slides.title: Two profiles with the same face
slides.objective: Avoid judging authenticity from copied profile details
screen_text: Which details can be copied?
How would you contact Aina independently?
slides.evidence: Two fictional profiles with same initials, employer and project details.
slides.interaction: Compare profiles; select verify rather than guessing.
slides.reveal: Use the established directory/contact.
slides.facilitator_notes: No score for guessing from account age or follower counts.
slides.what_this_shows: Two profiles with the same photo, name and posts. Can you tell which is real?
slides.key_point: You cannot tell from the screen. Photos, names, posts and follower counts can all be copied. Contact the person through the staff directory.

slides.title: A genuine account, an unusual request
screen_text: The account may be real.
The request still needs authorisation.
slides.evidence: Known colleague account asks for a staff contact list.
slides.interaction: Reveal request, then ask how to verify need and permitted disclosure.
slides.reveal: Follow data-sharing rules and independently verify the purpose.
slides.facilitator_notes: Let the room read the chat. Ask what the request would disclose before showing the findings.
slides.what_this_shows: A real colleague’s account asks Aina for the full staff contact list.
slides.key_point: A genuine account can still be used by someone else, and even a genuine request needs permission.

slides.reveal: Follow data-sharing rules and independently verify the purpose.
slides.interaction: Ask how to verify the need and what may be disclosed; then explain the diagram.
slides.title: Two checks before sharing the list
slides.objective: Separate verifying the purpose from permitted disclosure, and account takeover from profile cloning
screen_text: Verify the purpose separately
Follow data-sharing rules
Copied profile or taken-over account
slides.evidence: Two findings and a diagram comparing a copied profile with a taken-over account.
slides.facilitator_notes: Distinguish account compromise from profile cloning. Both can send the same message, so both need an independent check.
slides.what_this_shows: What Aina does with the request, and why a known account is not proof of who is typing.
slides.key_point: Verify the purpose separately and share only what is needed, through the approved route.

slides.title: The support page that found you
screen_text: An unsolicited support contact offers to fix an account issue.
slides.evidence: Search advert/social direct message pointing to fake brand support.
slides.interaction: Inspect claimed identity and route to known support.
slides.reveal: Start support from the known service/app.
slides.facilitator_notes: Do not suggest every advert is malicious.
slides.what_this_shows: Aina complains publicly about a login problem and “support” replies within minutes.
slides.key_point: If support found you, do not use it. Start from the app, your saved bookmark or your IT helpdesk.

slides.title: A collaboration that sounds relevant
slides.objective: Reassess a sensitive action after a normal conversation
screen_text: A normal conversation can lead to an unexpected request.
slides.evidence: Contact discusses a project before requesting a document/login.
slides.interaction: Reveal benign opener then sensitive follow-up.
slides.reveal: Re-evaluate when money, access or information is requested.
slides.facilitator_notes: Pair exercise: identify the point requiring verification. Keep business names fictional.
slides.what_this_shows: A friendly professional contact builds trust, then asks for a sign-in and internal documents.
slides.key_point: Re-check whenever a conversation reaches money, access or information, however friendly it has been.

slides.title: Someone is using your name
screen_text: Preserve the profile details.
Report and warn affected contacts through a trusted channel.
Use official account recovery if the genuine account is compromised.
slides.evidence: A copied profile sends requests to colleagues.
slides.interaction: Walk through the three responses; the sorting table follows.
slides.reveal: Password changes alone do not remove a copied profile.
slides.facilitator_notes: Internal security/communications owns work-related coordination. Avoid promising platform takedown times.
slides.what_this_shows: What to do when someone pretends to be you, and how that differs from someone taking over your account.
slides.key_point: Preserve the evidence, then report and warn affected contacts through a trusted channel.

slides.reveal: Password changes alone do not remove a copied profile.
slides.interaction: Sort cloning and takeover response cards.
slides.title: Copied profile or taken-over account?
slides.objective: Match each response action to cloning or takeover
screen_text: Which action fits which situation?
Password changes alone do not remove a copied profile.
slides.evidence: A tick table of four actions against the two situations.
slides.facilitator_notes: A password change secures the genuine account but does nothing about a separate copied profile. Avoid promising platform takedown times.
slides.what_this_shows: Which action fits which situation.
slides.key_point: A copied profile needs a platform report; a taken-over account needs official recovery. Both need you to warn contacts through a trusted channel.

slides.title: Verify before you classify
slides.objective: Choose a next action with uncertain identity
screen_text: A profile looks familiar, but the request is new.
slides.evidence: Aina’s apparent profile requests a work document.
slides.interaction: Choose: trust photo, continue in chat, verify through directory.
slides.reveal: Verify the request and permission to share.
slides.facilitator_notes: Ask learners to justify the route, not only the classification.

options.label: Trust the photo
options.feedback: Profile details can be copied.

options.label: Ask in the same chat
options.feedback: The person controlling that chat can answer.

options.label: Contact through the staff directory
options.feedback: Verify independently and check sharing permissions.

slides.what_this_shows: A familiar profile asks Farid for a supplier contract.
slides.key_point: Verify through the staff directory, then check the contract may be shared that way.

slides.title: Module 1 takeaways
screen_text: Photos, names and job titles are easy to copy.
A real account can be misused, and a real request can still need permission.
Re-check when a chat turns to money, access or information.
slides.facilitator_notes: Read the slide aloud briefly; it frames the module. No hidden content.
takeaways: Photos, names and job titles are easy to copy.
A real account can be misused, and a real request can still need permission.
Re-check when a chat turns to money, access or information.
slides.habit: Contact people through the directory, not through the message.
slides.what_this_shows: What to remember from Module 1.
slides.key_point: Contact people through the directory, not through the message.

slides.title: Short break
screen_text: Short break
We return with Module 2 · The trusted request
slides.facilitator_notes: Break. Restart on time; nothing advances automatically.

slides.title: Module 2: The trusted request
slides.objective: What this module covers and why it matters.
screen_text: Name the pressure tactics in an urgent request
Pause politely without refusing outright
Verify payments and calls through records you already hold
slides.facilitator_notes: Read the slide aloud briefly; it frames the module. No hidden content.
slides.why: Attackers borrow authority and urgency because people want to help their manager and meet deadlines.
outcomes: Name the pressure tactics in an urgent request
Pause politely without refusing outright
Verify payments and calls through records you already hold
slides.what_this_shows: What this module covers and why it matters.
slides.key_point: Urgency and authority are reasons to check, not reasons to skip the check.

slides.title: An urgent request from the manager
screen_text: The deadline is close.
The normal approval process still applies.
slides.evidence: Ravi’s display name requests an exceptional purchase.
slides.interaction: Reveal request and secrecy instruction.
slides.reveal: Confirm through established work channels.
slides.facilitator_notes: Connect to opening without replaying its six slides.
slides.what_this_shows: “Ravi” asks Farid to pay a new supplier now and approve it later.
slides.key_point: Normal approval still applies when the deadline is close. Confirm with Ravi on his directory number.

slides.title: What the pressure asks you to skip
screen_text: Urgency
Secrecy
An exception to normal approval
slides.evidence: Fictional message: “Handle this before the meeting; I’ll approve later.”
slides.interaction: Identify the business check being bypassed.
slides.reveal: The risk is the requested exception, even if the person is genuine.
slides.facilitator_notes: Discuss authority, fear and helpfulness without stereotyping victims.
slides.what_this_shows: The three pressure tactics hidden in one short message.
slides.key_point: Urgency, secrecy and “I’ll approve it later” all try to remove a check. The risk is the exception, even if the sender is genuine.

slides.title: A polite way to pause
screen_text: “I can help once I confirm through our normal approval process.”
slides.evidence: Pairs act as employee and impatient requester.
slides.interaction: Two-minute roleplay, swap, debrief.
slides.reveal: Choose a specific verification route and next step.
slides.facilitator_notes: Make room for cultural/authority concerns. Managers should support this behaviour.
slides.what_this_shows: Practise saying “not yet” politely to someone senior.
slides.key_point: Name the route and the next step: “I’ll call you back on your directory number, then raise it for approval.”

slides.title: The voice on the phone
screen_text: A caller knows your name and manager.
They ask for an account reset or code.
slides.evidence: Scripted caller claims IT support.
slides.interaction: Read a captioned script; ask what proves identity.
slides.reveal: Call the established service desk.
slides.facilitator_notes: No voice cloning of real people required. Do not collect codes.
slides.what_this_shows: A caller knows Aina’s name and manager, and asks her to read out a code.
slides.key_point: Knowing names proves nothing. Hang up and call the service desk on its known number. Never read out a sign-in code.

slides.title: What proves who is calling?
slides.objective: State the response to a caller who knows names and asks for a reset or a code
screen_text: Knowing names does not prove identity.
Hang up.
Call the service desk using its known number.
Never read out a sign-in code.
slides.interaction: Read the statement and the three actions; ask the room which number they would call.
slides.facilitator_notes: This is the lesson from the call on the previous slide. Do not collect codes; nobody reads one out, even as a demonstration.
slides.what_this_shows: What to do when a caller asks for a reset or a code.
slides.key_point: Knowing names does not prove identity. Hang up, call the service desk using its known number, and never read out a sign-in code.

slides.title: A face or voice cannot approve a payment
slides.objective: Use business controls for synthetic-media risk
screen_text: Verify the transaction through a separate authorised process.
slides.evidence: Reference the Hong Kong case from opening plus a fictional manager call.
slides.interaction: Compare cosmetic detection with independent verification.
slides.reveal: Visual glitches are insufficient as the only defence.
slides.facilitator_notes: Do not claim all synthetic media is detectable or all video calls are unsafe.
slides.what_this_shows: Why spotting a fake video is not a reliable defence.
slides.key_point: Do not rely on spotting glitches. A separate, authorised payment process works whether the video is real or fake.

slides.title: Which number will you call?
screen_text: The email includes a new phone number to confirm new bank details.
slides.evidence: Old vendor record, new email signature and directory contact.
slides.interaction: Choose callback destination, explain rationale.
slides.reveal: Use established records; do not rely on a number supplied with the change.
slides.facilitator_notes: The genuine vendor may have a new number too; update records through approved procedure.

options.label: New number in the email
options.feedback: It comes from the same unverified request.

options.label: Existing vendor record
options.feedback: Use the established contact and required approval.

options.label: Wait without telling anyone
options.feedback: Hold the action and notify the appropriate owner.

slides.what_this_shows: A bank-change email gives Farid a new number to call.
slides.key_point: Call the number already in your records, never one supplied with the change.

slides.title: Keep the process when the request is genuine
slides.objective: Avoid labelling all sensitive requests as fraud
screen_text: A verified vendor really has changed banks.
slides.evidence: Established contact confirms change; approval is still pending.
slides.interaction: Ask whether verification alone permits payment.
slides.reveal: Complete authorised approval and record updates.
slides.facilitator_notes: Explicit legitimate example. Verification and authorisation serve different purposes.

options.label: Pay immediately after the call
options.feedback: Identity verification does not replace payment authorisation.

options.label: Complete the approved bank-change and payment process
options.feedback: Proceed only after verification, records and approvals are complete.

options.label: Treat every bank change as fraud
options.feedback: A verified legitimate change can proceed through the proper process.

slides.what_this_shows: The supplier confirms the bank change is real. Can Farid pay now?
slides.key_point: Verification checks who is asking. Authorisation decides whether it may happen. A genuine change still goes through approval.

slides.title: Module 2 takeaways
screen_text: Urgency, secrecy and “approve it later” are pressure tactics.
A face, a voice or a caller’s inside knowledge does not prove identity.
Genuine requests still follow the approval process.
slides.facilitator_notes: Read the slide aloud briefly; it frames the module. No hidden content.
takeaways: Urgency, secrecy and “approve it later” are pressure tactics.
A face, a voice or a caller’s inside knowledge does not prove identity.
Genuine requests still follow the approval process.
slides.habit: Call back on a number you already have before you pay, reset or share.
slides.what_this_shows: What to remember from Module 2.
slides.key_point: Call back on a number you already have before you pay, reset or share.

slides.title: Module 3: The message that fits your job
slides.objective: What this module covers and why it matters.
screen_text: Find the action a message is asking you to take
Read sender addresses and links without opening them
Recognise “safety signs” that prove nothing
slides.facilitator_notes: Read the slide aloud briefly; it frames the module. No hidden content.
slides.why: The most convincing messages look like ordinary work: an invitation, a shared file, an account notice.
outcomes: Find the action a message is asking you to take
Read sender addresses and links without opening them
Recognise “safety signs” that prove nothing
slides.what_this_shows: What this module covers and why it matters.
slides.key_point: Ask three questions of every message: who is asking, what would I authorise, and how can I check outside this message?

slides.title: A message that fits your work
screen_text: Who is asking?
What would I authorise or disclose?
How can I verify outside this message?
slides.evidence: Meeting, benefits and document invitations.
slides.interaction: Ask which action creates risk.
slides.reveal: Use context, action and independent route together.
slides.facilitator_notes: Do not claim most breaches start with spear phishing.
slides.what_this_shows: Three ordinary work messages, each asking for a different risky action.
slides.key_point: Look for the action: sign in, share data, open a file. Then verify outside the message. Any of these could be genuine.

slides.title: The sender behind the display name
slides.objective: Inspect sender without treating it as conclusive
screen_text: Expand the sender.
Check the full address and reply destination.
slides.evidence: Manager display name with a different reserved .example address.
slides.interaction: Toggle sender details.
slides.reveal: A mismatch may be a clue; a match still needs request verification.
slides.facilitator_notes: Explain sender spoofing, lookalike domains and compromised accounts in notes, not as a protocol lecture.
slides.what_this_shows: What the full sender address reveals behind the display name.
slides.key_point: A mismatched address is a warning sign, but a matching one does not prove safety. Verify the request itself.

slides.title: The destination behind the label
screen_text: Preview without opening.
Find the actual hostname.
slides.evidence: Display https://login.company.example.attacker.test/review as inert text.
slides.interaction: Highlight hostname parts after vote.
slides.reveal: Hostname ends with attacker.test.
slides.facilitator_notes: Reserved .test domain. Genuine hosting and redirects can also be abused. Never navigate.
slides.what_this_shows: Who really controls this link? Vote, then see how to read it.
slides.key_point: Read the web address from the right, up to the first single slash. The last part, attacker.test, owns the site.

slides.title: A polished message can still deceive
screen_text: Professional writing and a familiar logo do not establish intent.
slides.evidence: Two polished messages: legitimate HR notice and deceptive approval request.
slides.interaction: Ask what business verification each requires.
slides.reveal: Focus on the action and context.
slides.facilitator_notes: AI can improve lure writing, but do not label a sample AI-generated without evidence.
slides.what_this_shows: Two professional-looking messages: one genuine, one deceptive.
slides.key_point: Polish and logos prove nothing. Judge the action requested and check it in the system you normally use.

slides.title: The same request on a phone
screen_text: The screen shows less detail.
Open the known application directly.
slides.evidence: SMS or WhatsApp notification requesting account review.
slides.interaction: Ask where Aina would check this; the inspection follows.
slides.reveal: Use the known service and report suspicious requests.
slides.facilitator_notes: Do not suggest mobile is inherently unsafe.
slides.what_this_shows: The same request arrives as a text message. Where would Aina check it?
slides.key_point: A sender label does not verify the sender. Open the app or website yourself instead of tapping the message.

slides.reveal: Use the known service and report suspicious requests.
slides.interaction: Compare the sender label and the link with the saved portal.
slides.title: The same text message, inspected
slides.objective: Compare the sender label and the link with the saved portal
screen_text: Sender label: MERANTI-IT
Message link against the saved IT portal
Independent check
slides.evidence: The SMS inspected: sender label, message link, saved portal address.
slides.facilitator_notes: The saved portal address is a fictional scenario detail. Do not suggest mobile is inherently unsafe; it compresses detail.
slides.what_this_shows: The sender label and the link, compared with the saved portal.
slides.key_point: The label is not identity, and the link does not match the saved portal. A short link gives little to compare, so open the saved portal instead.

slides.title: A QR code moves the request
slides.objective: Treat QR as a route requiring verification
screen_text: Where would this code take you?
Did you initiate this sign-in or linking action?
slides.evidence: Mock account-security email with an inert QR tile.
slides.interaction: Reveal destination in the deck, not via phone scan.
slides.reveal: Use the known portal instead of an unsolicited request.
slides.facilitator_notes: No functional login/linking QR. Distinguish URL phishing from device-linking later.
slides.what_this_shows: A QR code that moves a sign-in request onto your phone.
slides.key_point: Treat a QR code like a link you cannot read. Use the known portal instead.

slides.title: A shared file is still a request
screen_text: Branding and file format do not establish safety.
slides.evidence: PDF/HTML/SVG file card and shared-document invitation.
slides.interaction: Select inspection cards; no file opens.
slides.reveal: Verify the sharing context before unexpected login/download.
slides.facilitator_notes: Keep attachment behaviour inert. File formats are examples, not automatic malicious classifications.
slides.what_this_shows: Shared files and attachments that lead to a sign-in or download.
slides.key_point: A file type or brand does not make it safe. If you did not expect it, check with the sender through a known contact first.

slides.title: Would you approve this?
slides.objective: Apply process to both genuine and deceptive requests
screen_text: Proceed, verify or report?
Explain the next action.
slides.evidence: Four cards: genuine bank change, compromised colleague, genuine portal IT notice, fake manager exception.
slides.interaction: Table groups select an action for each.
slides.reveal: Independent verification may be right for genuine sensitive requests too.
slides.facilitator_notes: Use EXERCISES.md answer key. Score process, not number of messages called malicious.
slides.what_this_shows: Four realistic requests: decide for each whether to proceed, verify first, or hold and report.
slides.key_point: Some requests are genuine. The right answer depends on the action and the route, not on calling everything phishing.

slides.title: The signals that do not prove safety
screen_text: Familiar logo
Known sender
HTTPS or no email warning
slides.evidence: Three claimed assurances plus optional fluent wording and MFA.
slides.interaction: Reveal what each signal establishes and its limit.
slides.reveal: Appearance, delivery and authentication do not validate the business request.
slides.facilitator_notes: Do not imply HTTPS is useless. It protects a connection to the destination.

slides.title: Module 4: Beyond the password
slides.objective: What this module covers, and the words we will use.
screen_text: Explain what an approval actually grants
Respond to sign-in prompts you did not start
Recognise code, app-permission and device-linking tricks
slides.facilitator_notes: Read the slide aloud briefly; it frames the module. No hidden content.
slides.why: Attackers no longer need your password if you approve a sign-in, a code, an app or a device for them.
outcomes: Explain what an approval actually grants
Respond to sign-in prompts you did not start
Recognise code, app-permission and device-linking tricks
slides.what_this_shows: What this module covers and why it matters.
slides.key_point: Before approving anything, ask: what does this give, and to whom? Did I start it?

slides.title: Words we will use
slides.objective: Define the module’s terms in plain language before the scenes
screen_text: MFA
Session
Device code
App permission
Linked device
Phishing-resistant MFA
slides.facilitator_notes: Read the six words briefly; point back to this slide whenever a term comes up.
slides.what_this_shows: Six words for this module, in plain language.
slides.key_point: You do not need the technical detail. For each one, ask what it gives, and to whom.
glossary: A second check when you sign in, such as an app prompt or a code
Staying signed in after you log in, so you are not asked again
A short code that signs another device in to your account
Letting an app read or change your mail and files
Another phone or computer that can use your account
Security keys or passkeys that only work on the real site

slides.title: Access can be granted without sharing a password
screen_text: A sign-in, permission or device approval can grant access.
slides.evidence: Four inert cards: login session, MFA request, app permission, linked device.
slides.interaction: Identify the access each card represents.
slides.reveal: Check what session, device or app receives access.
slides.facilitator_notes: Keep technical protocol detail in notes.
slides.what_this_shows: Four ways to give someone access without sharing a password.
slides.key_point: A session, an MFA approval, an app permission or a linked device can each let someone act as you.

slides.title: The login session an attacker can reuse
slides.objective: Understand session theft at a high level
screen_text: A deceptive sign-in flow may capture a usable session.
slides.evidence: Annotated static sign-in sequence, no credential fields.
slides.interaction: Reveal the access consequence.
slides.reveal: Use approved sign-in routes and report suspicious flows.
slides.facilitator_notes: Describe AiTM conceptually. No proxy code or live capture. Do not say MFA is pointless.
slides.what_this_shows: How a fake sign-in page can capture a working login, even with MFA.
slides.key_point: Sign in from your bookmark or app, not from a link. Phishing-resistant MFA, such as security keys and passkeys, blocks this relay.

slides.title: An approval you did not start
screen_text: Deny an unexpected request.
Report repeated or suspicious prompts.
slides.evidence: Mock approval notification repeated twice.
slides.interaction: Choose deny/report or approve-to-stop.
slides.reveal: Do not approve access you did not initiate.
slides.facilitator_notes: MFA remains useful. Number matching reduces some risks but does not legitimise an unsolicited request.
slides.what_this_shows: Sign-in prompts arrive late at night while Aina is not signing in.
slides.key_point: Deny any prompt you did not start and report it. Never approve just to make the prompts stop.

slides.title: A real sign-in page, someone else’s code
screen_text: Whose device or session would this code authorise?
slides.evidence: Document invitation supplies a DEMO-ONLY code and genuine-looking static service page.
slides.interaction: Show the message and the genuine page; ask the question before the next slide answers it.
slides.reveal: Enter codes only for recognised sessions you initiated.
slides.facilitator_notes: No real device code. Verify purpose even when the service address is genuine.
slides.what_this_shows: A genuine sign-in page asks for a code that someone else sent Aina.
slides.key_point: Only enter and authorise a code for a sign-in you started yourself.

slides.reveal: Enter codes only for recognised sessions you initiated.
slides.interaction: Reveal who initiated the request.
slides.title: Whose device the code would sign in
slides.objective: Show where the code came from and what authorising it does
screen_text: The sender’s device started a sign-in
Aina enters the code and authorises
Their device gets access
slides.evidence: Diagram: sender’s device, the code, the real page, access granted.
slides.facilitator_notes: No real device code. Verify purpose even when the service address is genuine.
slides.what_this_shows: Where the code came from, and what authorising it would do.
slides.key_point: Here, authorising the code would sign in the sender’s device as Aina. Authorise only sign-ins you started yourself.

slides.title: The app asking for your permission
screen_text: An app asks to read messages or files.
Use the approved application process.
slides.evidence: Fictional Meeting Helper requests unnecessary access.
slides.interaction: Inspect permission list, choose IT approval route.
slides.reveal: A real consent screen does not validate the app’s purpose.
slides.facilitator_notes: Unknown publisher alone is not definitive. Do not ask learners to grant real consent.
slides.what_this_shows: A meeting app asks for far more access than it needs.
slides.key_point: A real permission screen does not make the app trustworthy. Ask IT to approve apps through the normal process.

slides.title: Linking another device
screen_text: Link only devices and sessions you recognise and initiated.
slides.evidence: Inert WhatsApp-style linked-device screen; fictional invitation.
slides.interaction: Show the invitation and what the app asks; the comparison follows.
slides.reveal: A linking QR can authorise access to an account.
slides.facilitator_notes: Use labelled nonfunctional placeholder, never a scannable account-link code.
slides.what_this_shows: An invitation says “join”, but the app asks to link a device.
slides.key_point: This invitation says “join”, but the app asks to link a device. Check your linked-devices list if unsure.

slides.reveal: A linking QR can authorise access to an account.
slides.interaction: Reveal difference between joining a group and linking a device.
slides.title: Joining a group or linking a device?
slides.objective: Contrast joining a conversation with linking a device to an account
screen_text: Joining a group
Linking a device
Link only devices you own and set up yourself
slides.evidence: Diagram: joining a group versus linking a device.
slides.facilitator_notes: Present linking as general product behaviour, not a sourced incident.
slides.what_this_shows: Joining adds you to one conversation. Linking gives another device your account.
slides.key_point: Linking gives another device ongoing access to your account. Link only devices you own and set up yourself.

slides.title: A defence that stopped the attempted access
screen_text: Cloudflare reported three credential submissions.
Hardware-key requirements prevented the attempted access.
slides.evidence: July 2022 SMS campaign, disclosed August 2022.

slides.reveal: Staff reporting and technical controls work together.
slides.facilitator_notes: Historical positive case. Do not promise keys prevent consent or payment fraud.
slides.what_this_shows: A real case where staff entered passwords but security keys stopped the attack.
slides.key_point: Strong controls and quick reporting work together. Some MFA types resist phishing much better than others.

slides.title: What does this approval grant?
screen_text: A trusted service asks you to approve an unfamiliar session.
slides.evidence: Genuine-looking code/consent/MFA mini-cards.

slides.what_this_shows: A trusted service asks you to approve an unfamiliar session.
slides.key_point: Check where the request came from through a route you know. If you did not start it, deny it and report it.

slides.title: Module 4 takeaways
screen_text: Approvals, codes, apps and linked devices can all grant access.

slides.title: Module 5: The helpful stranger
slides.objective: What this module covers and why it matters.

Stop when a web page asks you to run something
Tell genuine support from a fake offer
slides.facilitator_notes: Read the slide aloud briefly; it frames the module. No hidden content.

outcomes: Check a support request before giving access
Stop when a web page asks you to run something
Tell genuine support from a fake offer

slides.interaction: Reveal display name and request.
slides.reveal: Verify a support ticket through the established helpdesk.
slides.facilitator_notes: This is a separate scene, not proof the earlier fraud caused an account issue.

slides.key_point: Verify a support offer with the helpdesk through a route you know. A name and photo in chat prove nothing.

slides.title: Remote access changes the stakes
screen_text: Who will control the device?
Which approved support request does this match?
slides.evidence: Unsolicited screen-control request.
slides.interaction: Choose directory/helpdesk verification.
slides.reveal: Use approved support workflow before access.
slides.facilitator_notes: Legitimate remote tools can be abused. No live remote session.

options.label: Accept control because the tool is well known
options.feedback: A legitimate tool can still enable unauthorised access.

options.label: Verify the ticket through the established helpdesk
options.feedback: Check support identity, purpose and authorised access before proceeding.

options.label: Send a login code to prove the account
options.feedback: Do not disclose codes to an unsolicited caller.

slides.what_this_shows: A remote-control request appears on Aina’s screen.
slides.key_point: No ticket, no session. Check with the helpdesk first, and never send a login code to prove anything.

slides.title: The verification page asks too much
screen_text: A page tells you to open an operating-system tool.
slides.evidence: Fake CAPTCHA panel; action labelled STOP: demo only.
slides.interaction: Show the page; ask what the step would do before the next slide answers it.
slides.reveal: Stop and contact approved support.
slides.facilitator_notes: No command, clipboard action or runnable payload in the mock-up.
slides.what_this_shows: A fake “are you human?” check ends by asking you to run something on your computer.
slides.key_point: No real check asks you to open a system tool and paste text.

slides.reveal: Stop and contact approved support.
slides.interaction: Reveal the request to run a supposed verification action.
slides.title: What that step would actually do
slides.objective: Explain what pasting a page’s text into a system tool can cause, and what to do
screen_text: Pasted text can execute instructions
Possible harm: data theft or remote control
Stop. Contact IT using your known route.
slides.evidence: Consequence diagram for the paste step.
slides.facilitator_notes: Outcomes are possible, not guaranteed: they depend on what ran and what was blocked.
slides.what_this_shows: What pasting the page’s text into a system tool could do, and what to do instead.
slides.key_point: Stop, close the page and contact IT. If anything already ran, report it immediately.

slides.title: A browser problem becomes a repair request

slides.evidence: CrashFix concept reconstruction, not exact malicious artefact.
slides.interaction: Reveal installation, delay, problem, repair pretext.
slides.reveal: Use approved software and support routes.
slides.facilitator_notes: Do not reproduce extension code. Cite Microsoft; do not invent losses.
slides.what_this_shows: A documented technique: a fake extension breaks your browser, then offers a harmful “fix”.
slides.key_point: Install software and get fixes only through approved sources and your IT team.

slides.title: The notice asks you to call
screen_text: An unexpected renewal notice includes a support number.
slides.evidence: Fictional subscription email with number shown as DEMO-NUMBER.
slides.interaction: Select a trusted account/support route.
slides.reveal: Check the known service, not the supplied callback number.
slides.facilitator_notes: Keep calls simulated. No operational phone numbers.

slides.key_point: Check the account through the service or team you already know, not the number in the notice.

slides.title: Which support request can you proceed with?
slides.objective: Recognise a legitimate verified support process

slides.evidence: Mei’s identity and session match the independently checked ticket.
slides.interaction: Choose permitted next step under support policy.

options.feedback: The known ticket confirms context; access and data rules still apply.

options.label: Give unrestricted control and all files
options.feedback: Verified support does not remove access limits.

options.label: Reject all help even for a verified ticket
options.feedback: Approved support can proceed under the normal policy.

slides.what_this_shows: This time the support request matches a ticket Aina raised herself.
slides.key_point: Verified help can go ahead under normal rules: stay present and share only what the fix needs.

slides.title: Module 5 takeaways
screen_text: Unrequested help is a warning sign.
Never run instructions that a web page gives you.
Genuine support can be checked and still follows the rules.

screen_text: Operations
Finance
Manager
IT support

A short report

slides.title: Evidence 1: the document invitation
screen_text: Aina receives a document invitation after a normal conversation.
slides.evidence: Card T1.
slides.interaction: Record known facts, unknowns and next action.
slides.reveal: Use a known route before access or disclosure.

slides.what_this_shows: Evidence card 1: a document invitation after a normal call.

slides.title: Evidence 2: the account approval

slides.interaction: Choose immediate report and the IT owner.

slides.what_this_shows: Evidence card 2: Aina admits she entered a code.
